title: The Opening
hookLine: the seven verses Muslims recite in every prayer (Quran 1)
tomorrow: a surah of three verses swears by time. what does it say?

cards: A song through a neighbor's wall, a line a grandmother hummed: a sound can be familiar for years before its meaning is.
Stand near a mosque at prayer time, or near a family praying at home, and you may hear seven short verses in Arabic, aloud or under the breath.
Those verses answer yesterday's question: al-Fatiha, the Opening, the first surah of the Quran.
A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Bukhari's collection is plain about it: there is no prayer without the Opening of the Book.

teach.b: Here's a story to hear it by.
In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that God said: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant, in two halves, and My servant will have what he asks.
Then it goes verse by verse, like a call and an answer. The worshipper says, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds," and God says, My servant has praised Me.
The worshipper names Him the Beneficent, the Merciful, and God says, My servant has extolled Me.
Then the middle line: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. This, God says, is between Me and My servant.
And the asking: "Show us the straight path." This is for My servant, and he shall have what he asked. So, in this hadith, al-Fatiha isn't only recited.

It's a conversation, said in every prayer, with an answer to every line. And a detail to pass on: the Quran itself speaks of seven oft-repeated verses, and a hadith in Bukhari names them as this surah.
A guest can listen for its shape: praise, then the turn to Thee alone, then the asking.

how: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in each of the daily prayers; in congregation the imam recites and those praying behind him listen or recite with him, depending on the school of law.

games.q: you're visiting a friend's family at prayer time and they invite you to sit and listen. which detail helps you follow the Opening?
o: listen for praise first, then 'Thee alone,' then the asking.
listen for the prophets' names; the Opening lists them in order.
listen for the call to prayer; the Opening uses the same words.
games.why: al-Fatiha moves from praise, to 'Thee alone we worship,' to 'show us the straight path'; in Sahih Muslim 395 it's split between God and the servant.

practice: Read one line slowly, aloud or under your breath: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Then leave a long silence after it, the space where, in the hadith, an answer comes.
If you pray, you can stay in that silence as prayer; if not, read it as a guest and simply listen to the quiet after the words.

Sahih al-Bukhari 756 (there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book)
